investingLive Americas FX news wrap 18 Nov: Waller/Fed minutes put a bigger December hike in play
body: The Fed’s October minutes put the size of the December move in focus. Almost all participants saw further hikes as likely under their baseline outlooks, and a couple were open to more than 25 basis points if inflation data disappointed. The 2-year yield edged higher, while the oil selloff helped pull longer-term yields lower. The 10-year still ended the U.S. session near 5.07%. Monetary Policy:

Stocks split. The Dow dropped more than 1% and the S&P 500 posted its fifth straight decline, while the Nasdaq Composite and Russell 2000 each gained about 0.4%. Nvidia gave back its early gains despite a beat and stronger guidance. That puts even more attention on Anthropic’s IPO as the next test of demand for AI shares.

The USD rose against six of the seven major currencies in the late snapshot. It gained the most against sterling, about 0.49%, and lost ground against the yen, with USDJPY essentially flat at 159.35 after rounding. GBPUSD traded at 1.3144 and EURUSD at 1.0973. UK headline CPI rose to 3.6% as expected, but softer-than-forecast services inflation trimmed December Bank of England hike odds and weighed on sterling. investinglive.com

The 2-year held up as traders weighed a larger December hike. Further out, the drop in oil helped take some pressure off yields. The 2-year and 10-year spread narrowed by about 5 basis points to 26 basis points.
The Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Russell 2000 figures are final closes.

Nvidia reported adjusted EPS of $2.68 versus $2.48 expected and revenue of $115.8 billion versus $109.0 billion expected. It guided to about $130 billion in quarterly revenue, yet shares reversed lower as uncertainty around the leadership transition and the financing of the AI buildout lingered. The chip index slipped, with Intel and Micron lower and AMD higher. images.investinglive.com

Energy and materials were among the laggards as crude and metals fell. Retail had some standouts of its own. Target rose on a stronger holiday outlook, and TJX gained after lifting its annual sales forecast. Walmart reports Thursday. marketwatch.com
Miners led the declines as copper weakened, and lower crude weighed on energy shares.

The October vote to hold was 10–2, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike. The minutes showed that some other participants also favored raising rates and a few who backed the hold saw it as a close call. A couple said a move larger than 25 basis points could be warranted in December if inflation data came in unfavorably. The minutes predate the October CPI report, which showed core prices rising 0.3% on the month. InvestingLive reported about 27 basis points priced for December and 62 across the next three meetings. Monetary Policy:

Waller made the case for a 50-basis-point hike or a stronger signal that more tightening is coming. His concern is that households and businesses start treating 3% inflation as normal when roughly 70% of core services components are already running above that pace. Barr backed further hikes if the economy performs as expected. Daly pointed to a stable labor market and resilient spending even among lower-income households, giving the Fed room to keep its focus on inflation. images.investinglive.com

December WTI settled at $83.26, down 3.20%, and the late screen showed $82.08, down 4.57%. U.S. crude inventories rose 3.38 million barrels versus 58,000 expected, while gasoline stocks jumped 5.19 million barrels. Shipping risks around the Strait of Hormuz persisted and talks with Iranian mediators continued. The inventory builds and surplus concerns carried more weight in Wednesday’s trade. investinglive.com

Gold traded near $3,727.39, down 3.17%, and silver fell 4.78% to $45.11. The firmer dollar and higher 2-year yield were headwinds for gold even as longer yields eased. Silver’s steeper drop came alongside weakness in industrial metals. images.investinglive.com
Bitcoin fell 3.72% to $62,462 late in the session. It traded more like metals and other heavily sold assets than the Nasdaq, which managed a gain.

The 2-year yield is the barometer for the December debate. A further rise would signal traders are putting more weight on a bigger hike. For stocks, Anthropic’s IPO pricing will test appetite for AI exposure after Nvidia’s reversal, while Walmart’s results will give traders another read on holiday spending. In crude, watch whether sellers can extend the inventory-driven break as Hormuz supply risks persist.

news.title: Kashkari says markets see more Fed hikes than officials do as four Fed voices turn hawkish
body: Hawkish Fed remarks arriving one after another should support the US dollar and keep front-end Treasury yields firm going into December. Gold is the asset most exposed. Through this cycle it has fallen as Fed hike expectations build, so more tightening talk is a headwind rather than a bid. For the Australian dollar, which is already near 10-month lows, a Fed that keeps hiking narrows the policy gap with the RBA. That raises the stakes for today’s Australian jobs data. If Kashkari is right that the shocks behind inflation are supply-driven, oil remains the key input to watch, because further energy price spikes would strengthen the hawks’ case.
When a voting Fed official says markets expect more hikes than his colleagues do and makes no effort to push back, the message is that the policy path may have to rise to meet the pricing.

Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Neel Kashkari said on Wednesday that markets believe the Fed will have to raise interest rates further than officials currently expect, a notable remark from a policymaker who votes on the Federal Open Market Committee this year. He made no attempt, in the comments reported, to talk that pricing down.

Kashkari traced the current bout of elevated inflation to a series of supply shocks and said the Fed’s priority must be keeping inflation expectations anchored. That framing matters. Central bankers often argue they can look through supply shocks, but only if the public keeps faith that inflation will return to target. When shocks arrive one after another, that faith becomes harder to take for granted, and Kashkari’s emphasis on expectations suggests he sees the risk as real rather than theoretical.

He also said the strength of demand has been a little surprising and described the labour market as resilient. Both points weaken the case for patience. A firm economy gives the Fed room to keep tightening without tipping it into a sharp downturn, and a resilient jobs market removes one of the main arguments a more cautious official might make for pausing. Kashkari added that interest rates can absolutely affect investment, pushing back on any suggestion that higher borrowing costs have lost their bite.

His comments landed on a day when several colleagues were sounding a similar note. Governor Christopher Waller, Governor Michael Barr and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly all struck hawkish tones on Wednesday, with Waller once again raising the possibility of a 50 basis point hike. A move of that size remains an outside possibility rather than the base case, but the fact that it is being discussed openly shows how far the debate has shifted toward the scale of further tightening rather than whether it is needed.

The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% at its late October meeting, with two officials dissenting in favour of a quarter point increase. Since then, hotter inflation data and a steady run of hawkish commentary have reinforced expectations of a hike at the December meeting.

Kashkari’s remark on market pricing is the one to watch. If officials begin publicly endorsing a higher path than their own projections imply, the December forecasts could shift up to meet the market, rather than the market moving back toward the Fed.

news.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Thursday, November 19, 2026: Australian jobs report preview
body: The Australian dollar goes into the release near 0.6715 (as I post at least), close to its weakest level since January, so the bar for a relief bounce is low. A solid headline gain plus a steady or lower jobless rate would likely bring back some pricing for a February hike and lift the Aussie off its lows. A rise in unemployment to 4.8% or higher would probably extend the slide and pull front-end yields lower as traders price a longer peak. The minutes flagged that oil costs tied to the Middle East conflict could add to inflation, which means a soft print alone may not close the door on further tightening while crude stays elevated.

--- Australia’s jobs report should recover most of September’s part-time losses, but with a divided RBA board split over how close the economy is to a sharper downturn, the unemployment rate matters more than the headline gain.

Australia’s October labour force report lands at 00:30 GMT on Thursday (7:30 pm US Eastern on Wednesday), and it arrives with more riding on it than a typical monthly print. Economists expect employment to have risen by around 25,000 after September’s surprise 39,300 fall, with the unemployment rate seen steady at 4.7%, a five-year high, and participation unchanged at 66.8%. Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics last month showed the decline was driven almost entirely by a 73,700 slump in part-time roles, while full-time jobs actually rose by about 34,000.

That split is the heart of the case for a rebound. CBA expects the part-time drop to reverse, arguing that large swings in part-time work have historically unwound the following month. Its own internal labour data point to October growth of around 18,000, which it describes as a touch below the pace needed to keep unemployment from rising. In other words, even a healthy-looking headline gain could leave the jobless rate drifting higher.

The release follows two days of mixed signals for the Reserve Bank of Australia. Minutes published on Tuesday showed six of nine board members backed November’s 25 basis point hike to 4.85%, the fifth increase of 2026 and the highest cash rate since 2008, judging policy not yet clearly tight enough to contain upside inflation risks. The three dissenters warned the economy might be close to a materially sharper downturn, pointing to the delayed effect of earlier hikes, a bigger-than-expected rise in unemployment and a softening housing market. Wednesday then brought September quarter wages up 1.1%, the largest quarterly gain since late 2023, lifting annual growth to 3.5%, although real wages have now gone backwards for four straight quarters with inflation above 4%.

The data matter because they speak directly to that split. A jobless rate stuck at 4.7%, or lower, would support the majority view that the labour market is loosening only gradually, which Westpac also expects as jobs growth runs below population growth. A rise to 4.8% or beyond would hand the dissenters fresh evidence and make it harder for the hawks to argue for a sixth hike. Several high-profile layoff announcements, including job cuts at NAB, Qantas, Rio Tinto and David Jones, add to the sense of downside risk, though economists note the numbers remain small relative to average monthly hiring.

The RBA’s own forecasts already assume unemployment climbs, reaching 4.9% by the end of this year and a bit above 5% by late 2028, so a modest uptick would not be a shock. The bigger question is the pace. Traders have largely abandoned bets on a December move, and CBA judges the 7 to 8 December meeting will not be live, flagging February as the next realistic window for another hike. A clean rebound in jobs alongside firm wages could keep that February door open, while a second soft month would push the conversation toward how long rates stay at their peak.
Watch the detail as closely as the headline: hours worked, the full-time versus part-time mix and the unrounded jobless rate will all shape how the board reads the print.

news.title: NZDUSD sellers stay in control as price nears the 0.54808 floor
body: The NZDUSD decline started on November 10 after the pair tested the upper channel trend line and turned lower, breaking below both its 200-hour and 100-hour moving averages. The go-ahead for more downside came the next day when the price bounced back to the 200-hour moving average and sellers leaned against it. That rejection set up six days of selling that took the pair to a low of 0.54808 yesterday.

Since then, the price has been consolidating. Yesterday’s bounce stalled at 0.55057, and today’s high reached nearly the same level at 0.5506. Today’s low came in at 0.5484, just above yesterday’s low. With the pair trading near 0.5488, the price is still closer to the floor of the range than the ceiling.

The 0.54808 low is the next level to get to and through. If the price breaks and stays below it, traders will look toward the lower channel trend line near 0.5465. A break through that line would give sellers more room to extend the move.

If buyers continue to lean against 0.54808, their first target is the top of the consolidation near 0.5506. Just above that sits the falling 100-hour moving average at 0.5512. Getting and staying above that moving average would give buyers their first technical victory and put the 200-hour moving average at 0.5550 in play. Buyers would need to clear that second moving average to take more control. Until then, the sellers keep the edge.

On November 10, the break below the moving averages shifted the bias lower. On November 11, the bounce back to the 200-hour moving average gave sellers a level to lean against. They could define their risk against that line. If the price had gotten back above it and held, the reason for leaning against it would have weakened.

The same thinking applies at 0.54808 today. Buyers leaning against the low can define their risk on a break below it. If the floor gives way and the price later bounces back to 0.54808, watch how it reacts. If sellers cap that bounce, the old floor starts to act as resistance. If buyers reclaim it and hold above it, the break may have failed. That retest can tell you which side is gaining control.

news.title: FOMC Minutes: A couple of participants noted a hike of more than 25 bps could warrant consideration in December
body: It sounds like Waller isn't alone in the 50 basis point hike camp.

The minutes show that the 10-2 vote understated how hawkish this meeting was. In Fed language “some” means more than “a few,” so Cook and Hammack had company among the non-voters. Add the participants who called it a close call and the bloc leaning toward a hike in October was substantial.

This was a conditional hold. Policymakers said outright that market pricing for December was doing part of the work, and several said that alignment was what made it safe to wait. Some of the hawks only accepted a hold because markets were already pricing more hikes.

The most important line is the one about more than 25 bps. A couple of participants said a bigger move could be considered if the inflation data came in unfavorable, and the October CPI did exactly that. Waller set a 0.3% core threshold for 50 bps, and the report met it. These minutes come before that report, so the case for a bigger move has only strengthened since.

The dovish argument rests on financial conditions. Mortgage rates are up, junk spreads have widened sharply, bank shares fell hard, and the market is taking a harder look at AI financing. A couple of officials argued for a gradual approach so households and businesses can adjust. That’s the case for 25 bps in December, but in these minutes it’s the minority view.

The market has 62 bps of hikes priced over the next three meetings, and nothing in these minutes argues against that. If anything, the debate has moved from whether the Fed hikes in December to how much with 27 bps priced in right now and 62 bps at the next three meetings.

news.title: Fed's Barr supports further rate hikes as inflation remains too high
body: Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said he supports raising interest rates further if the economy performs as expected, reinforcing his hawkish stance as policymakers struggle to bring inflation back to target.

Barr described the US economy as strong, with low unemployment, but warned that inflation remains too high and continues to put pressure on American families. He emphasized the importance of returning inflation to the Fed's 2% target in a timely manner.

The comments are consistent with his September remarks, when he argued that elevated energy prices and the surge in artificial intelligence investment were complicating the inflation outlook and likely requiring additional monetary tightening.
Barr nevertheless stopped short of committing to a specific timetable, saying incoming economic data would determine the Fed's next move.

His comments come amid an increasingly hawkish debate at the Fed. Policymakers have been grappling with stubborn inflation despite a resilient labor market, raising questions about whether current interest rates are sufficiently restrictive.

The key takeaway is that Barr sees little justification for easing monetary policy while inflation remains elevated. With the economy continuing to perform well, he appears prepared to support additional tightening to restore price stability.
The market is pricing in 61 bps in hikes in the next three meetings. The FOMC minutes are due at the top of the hour.

news.title: The US Treasury auctions $16B of 20 year bonds at a high year at 5.459%
body: The auction came in right at the when-issued yield, a modest improvement over the average 0.5-basis-point tail. Bid to cover matched the average. Direct bidders took a larger share than usual, but that only partly offset softer indirect demand, leaving dealers with a slightly larger share. The better pricing and mixed demand add up to an average auction.
